entry: Ribonucleoprotein particle found in most cells. It synthesizes [[Protein|proteins]] through [[Translation (biology)|translation]] of genetic information carried in messenger RNA (mRNA). During translation, the ribosome decodes successive codons in an mRNA molecule and, with the aid of transfer RNA (tRNA), links [[Amino acid|amino acids]] into a polypeptide chain. Each ribosome has a small and a large subunit, built from ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and many ribosomal proteins. Ribosomes differ in size and composition among [[Bacteria|bacteria]], [[Archaea|archaea]] and [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], but share a core structure that reflects a common evolutionary origin. Some antibiotics kill bacteria by inhibiting their ribosomes while leaving human ribosomes unaffected. First observed by George Emil Palade in 1955, ribosomes had their discovery recognized by the [[Nobel Prize]] in Physiology or Medicine in 1974, and the determination of their atomic structure and mechanism by the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009.

American retired [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestler]], known as the Nature Boy. Regarded by multiple peers and journalists as the greatest professional wrestler of all time, he headlined Starrcade, the premier annual NWA/WCW event, on 10 occasions. Flair spent much of his career with Jim Crockett Promotions and World Championship Wrestling (WCW), where he was the first holder of the WCW World Heavyweight Championship. He was the first two-time [[WWE]] Hall of Fame inductee. WWE recognizes him as a 16-time world champion, though counts vary from 16 to 25; the most widely accepted figure is 21, which Flair himself has claimed.

Mexican and American actor. Born in [[Mexico City]], he became a star in Mexico before working in American film and television. He played Armando in the *Planet of the Apes* films and the villain Khan Noonien Singh in *Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan* (1982). He played Mr. Roarke in the television series *Fantasy Island* and won an Emmy Award for the miniseries *How the West Was Won* (1978). For 13 years he was a spokesman for [[Chrysler]], appearing in commercials that extolled the "rich Corinthian leather" of the Cordoba.

English actor, film director and producer. As an actor, he is best remembered for *Brighton Rock* (1948), *The Great Escape* (1963) and *Jurassic Park* (1993). His film *Gandhi* (1983), which he directed, won Academy Awards for Best Picture and Best Director. His later films include *Chaplin* (1992), a biography of [[Charlie Chaplin]]. In 1952 he originated a role in the West End staging of [[Agatha Christie]]'s *The Mousetrap*, now the longest-running play in London. He was knighted in 1976 and served as president of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art and of the British Academy of Film and Television Arts (BAFTA).

American fashion and portrait photographer. Avedon specialized in capturing movement in still pictures of fashion, theater and dance, working for *Harper's Bazaar*, [[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]] and *Elle*. Born in [[New York City]] to a Jewish family, he enlisted in the United States Maritime Service in 1942 and became a staff photographer. He was later hired by *Harper's Bazaar* after meeting its art director, Alexey Brodovitch. An obituary in [[The New York Times]] said his photographs "helped define America's image of style, beauty and culture for the last half-century."

English business magnate. Branson co-founded the Virgin Group in 1970, starting with a mail-order record business and opening Virgin Records stores in 1972. He founded the Virgin Atlantic airline, the rail company Virgin Rail Group and the space tourism company Virgin Galactic in 2004. Branson has [[Dyslexia|dyslexia]] and started his first business, a magazine called *Student*, at 16. He was knighted in 2000 for services to entrepreneurship. In 2007 [[Time (magazine)|Time]] magazine named him one of the 100 Most Influential People in the World, and [[Forbes]] listed his estimated net worth at US$3 billion in 2023.

Welsh actor. Noted for his powerful presence and baritone voice, Burton established himself as a Shakespearean stage actor, playing Prince Hal, [[Hamlet]] and [[Othello]] early in his career. He received a Tony Award for Best Actor in a Musical for playing [[King Arthur]] in *Camelot* (1960). Despite seven Academy Award nominations, he never won an Oscar. He married [[Elizabeth Taylor]] twice, and they starred together in eleven films. Critic Kenneth Tynan called him "the natural successor to Olivier," but his heavy drinking fed a reputation as a great performer who had wasted his talent.

British evolutionary biologist and author. Dawkins popularized the gene-centered view of [[Evolution|evolution]] in *The Selfish Gene* (1976), in which he coined the word [[Meme|meme]]. *The Blind Watchmaker* (1986) explains how [[Natural selection|natural selection]] creates complexity. He was the first Simonyi Professor for the Public Understanding of Science at the [[University of Oxford]] from 1995 to 2008. Along with [[Christopher Hitchens]], Daniel Dennett and Sam Harris, he is known as one of the "Four Horsemen of New Atheism." His book *The God Delusion* (2006) made the case for atheism.

German mathematician. His best-known contribution is the Dedekind cut, a method of defining [[Real number|real numbers]] in which an irrational number divides the [[Rational number|rational numbers]] into two classes. He was also a pioneer of modern [[Set theory|set theory]] and of the [[Philosophy of mathematics|philosophy of mathematics]] known as logicism, and he made important contributions to number theory and [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]], particularly ring theory. Dedekind studied at the [[University of Göttingen]], where he became the last student of [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]]. He taught at the Polytechnic school in [[Zurich|Zürich]] from 1858 and returned to his native Braunschweig in 1862, where he spent the rest of his life. He retired in 1894 and never married.

American actor. Born in [[Brooklyn]], Dreyfuss emerged from the New Hollywood wave of the 1970s, starring in *American Graffiti* (1973), *Jaws* (1975) and *Close Encounters of the Third Kind* (1977). He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *The Goodbye Girl* (1977) and was nominated again for *Mr. Holland's Opus* (1995). On television he starred as the title character in the [[CBS]] drama *The Education of Max Bickford* and portrayed [[Bernie Madoff]] in the ABC miniseries *Madoff* (2016).

American theoretical physicist. He shared the 1965 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics with Julian Schwinger and Shin'ichirō Tomonaga for fundamental work in [[Quantum electrodynamics|quantum electrodynamics]] (QED). He also developed the path integral formulation of quantum mechanics and a pictorial scheme for particle interactions, now known as [[Feynman diagram|Feynman diagrams]]. During World War II he worked on the [[Manhattan Project]], helping develop the atomic bomb. He later served on the Rogers Commission investigating the [[Space Shuttle Challenger disaster]]. He is credited with pioneering [[Quantum computing|quantum computing]] and introducing the concept of [[Nanotechnology|nanotechnology]]. Through books and lectures, including *The Feynman Lectures on Physics* (1961–1964), he became a keen popularizer of physics.

Irish actor and singer. Harris rose to prominence as an icon of the British New Wave and won the [[Cannes Film Festival]] Award for Best Actor, and he was Oscar-nominated for *This Sporting Life* (1963). He played Albus Dumbledore in the first two films of the [[Harry Potter (film series)|Harry Potter]] series and King Arthur in *Camelot* (1967). In 1968 his recording of "MacArthur Park" topped charts in Australia, Jamaica and Canada. Educated by the [[Jesuits]], he was a talented [[Rugby union|rugby union]] player until he caught [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]] in his teens.

King of England from 1483 to 1485. The last king of the [[House of Plantagenet|Plantagenet]] dynasty, Richard served as Lord Protector for the 12-year-old Edward V before being proclaimed king. Two major rebellions marked his reign, and Edward V and his brother disappeared in the [[Tower of London|Tower of London]]. Richard was killed at the Battle of Bosworth Field, which marked the end of the Middle Ages in England. In 2012 a skeleton found beneath a [[Leicester]] car park was identified as his by [[Radiocarbon dating|radiocarbon dating]] and DNA, and he was reburied in Leicester Cathedral in 2015.

King of England from 1377 to 1399. Son of [[Edward the Black Prince]] and Joan of Kent, Richard succeeded his grandfather [[Edward III]] at the age of 10. He played a central part in suppressing the [[Peasants' Revolt]] of 1381. His dependence on a small circle of courtiers led to a takeover of government by the Lords Appellant in 1387. After taking revenge on the Appellants in 1397, Richard was deposed in 1399 by Henry Bolingbroke, who was crowned Henry IV. Richard is thought to have been starved to death in captivity. [[William Shakespeare|Shakespeare]]'s play *Richard II* shaped his posthumous reputation.

King of England from 1189 to 1199. Known as Richard the Lionheart for his reputation as a military leader, he was the son of [[Henry II of England|Henry II]] and [[Eleanor of Aquitaine]]. He also ruled as duke of Normandy, Aquitaine and Gascony, but spent little of his reign in England, which historians long viewed as a mere source of revenue for his armies. Modern scholars regard that view as anachronistic. He led the [[Third Crusade]] against [[Saladin]], winning several victories but failing to retake [[Jerusalem]]. Captured on his return and held for ransom, he was released in 1194. He spent his final years defending his French lands against [[Philip II of France]]. He died of [[Gangrene|gangrene]] after a [[Crossbow|crossbow]] wound received at the siege of Châlus.

37th president of the United States, from 1969 to 1974. A Republican, Nixon represented California in both houses of [[United States Congress|Congress]] and served as vice president under [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]] from 1953 to 1961. He reduced U.S. involvement in the [[Vietnam War]], opened relations with [[China]] after his 1972 visit, and pursued détente with the [[Soviet Union]]. The Apollo 11 Moon landing and the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency came during his term. He was re-elected in 1972 by one of the largest landslides in American history. The [[Watergate scandal]] led him to resign in 1974, making him the only U.S. president to resign. His successor, [[Gerald Ford]], granted him a controversial pardon. In retirement he wrote nine books and became an elder statesman on foreign affairs.

American stand-up comedian and actor. Regarded as one of the greatest and most influential comedians, Pryor drew on his own hardships in a raw, confessional style. He won five [[Grammy Awards]] and a Primetime Emmy Award, and in 1998 received the first Kennedy Center Mark Twain Prize for American Humor. As an actor he starred mainly in comedies, most notably with [[Gene Wilder]] in *Silver Streak* (1976) and *Stir Crazy* (1980). He co-wrote *Blazing Saddles* (1974) with [[Mel Brooks]]. After appearing on [[Saturday Night Live]] and [[Sesame Street]], he hosted *The Richard Pryor Show* (1977). He had [[Multiple sclerosis|multiple sclerosis]] in later life.

American serial killer and sex offender, known as the Night Stalker. From April 1984 to August 1985 Ramirez murdered at least 15 people during break-ins in Greater Los Angeles and the [[San Francisco Bay Area]]. His crimes were shaped partly by a cousin, a [[Vietnam War]] veteran, who taught him military skills. He cultivated an interest in [[Satanism]] and the occult and sometimes left [[Pentagram|pentagrams]] at crime scenes. In 1989 he was convicted of 13 murders, five attempted murders, 11 sexual assaults and 14 burglaries and was sentenced to death. He died of complications from B-cell lymphoma while awaiting execution.

German composer and conductor. A leading figure of the late Romantic and early modern era, Strauss was known for tone poems such as *Don Juan*, *Also sprach Zarathustra* and *Ein Heldenleben*, and for operas including *Salome*, *Elektra* and *Der Rosenkavalier*. As a conductor he was chiefly admired for his interpretations of Liszt, Mozart and Wagner. In 1920 he co-founded the Salzburg Festival. In 1933 he was appointed head of the Reichsmusikkammer and principal conductor of the Bayreuth Festival in [[Nazi Germany]]. Critics have seen this as collaboration with the [[Nazi Party]], but his apparent acquiescence is said to have protected his Jewish daughter-in-law and her children. He insisted on using the Jewish librettist Stefan Zweig for *Die schweigsame Frau*, which led to his dismissal from both posts in 1935. In 1948 a denazification tribunal in [[Munich]] cleared him of wrongdoing.

German composer, theater director and conductor, best known for his [[Opera|operas]], or music dramas. Wagner wrote both the libretti and the music for his stage works, seeking a Gesamtkunstwerk, or "total work of art," that united poetic, musical, visual and dramatic elements. His use of chromaticism and leitmotifs greatly influenced classical music, and *Tristan und Isolde* is regarded as an important precursor to modernist music. He had the Bayreuth Festspielhaus built to stage his mature works, and it hosted the premieres of *Der Ring des Nibelungen* and *Parsifal*. His operas and essays were controversial in his lifetime, and the extent of his [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]] remains debated. His operas remain central to the repertoire of major opera houses and concert halls worldwide.

Capital city of Virginia, United States (pop., 2020: 226,610). Richmond lies at the fall line of the James River and replaced Williamsburg as the colonial capital in 1780. The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, written by [[Thomas Jefferson]], was passed there. During the [[American Civil War]], Richmond was the capital of the [[Confederate States of America]]. Law, finance and government drive its economy, and it is one of about a dozen cities with both a U.S. Court of Appeals and a [[Federal Reserve]] bank.

Measure of the strength of [[Earthquake|earthquakes]]. Charles Richter developed it with Beno Gutenberg for local earthquakes in [[Southern California]], presenting it in a 1935 paper. Because the scale uses [[Logarithm|logarithms]], each whole-number increase in magnitude means a tenfold increase in measured [[Amplitude|amplitude]] and about 31.6 times more [[Energy|energy]]. Most seismologists now use the moment magnitude scale because of shortcomings in the original, although the news media still call such values "Richter" magnitudes.

English singer, songwriter, radio DJ and podcaster. His debut single "Never Gonna Give You Up" was a No. 1 hit in more than 25 countries and won the 1988 Brit Award for Best British Single. The album *Whenever You Need Somebody* (1987) sold 15 million copies. Astley retired in 1993 and returned in 2000. In 2007 he became an internet phenomenon through the [[Rickrolling]] meme, which uses the video for "Never Gonna Give You Up." The song reached one billion views on [[YouTube]] in 2021. He was nominated for a Grammy Award for Best New Artist in 1989 but lost to [[Tracy Chapman]].

American singer, songwriter and record producer. Born and raised in [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo]], James had his most successful album with *Street Songs* (1981), which included "Super Freak" and "Give It to Me Baby." He also wrote and produced for other artists, including [[Eddie Murphy]], Teena Marie and Smokey Robinson. MC Hammer's 1990 hit "U Can't Touch This" sampled "Super Freak," and James received his only [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] for composing it. Drug addiction, especially to [[Cocaine]], hurt his career, and in 1993 he was convicted of kidnapping and assaulting two women, receiving a three-year sentence. He died of [[Heart failure|heart failure]].

American record producer. Rubin co-founded Def Jam Recordings, founded American Recordings and was co-president of [[Columbia Records]]. He helped popularize [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] by producing [[LL Cool J]], the [[Beastie Boys]] and [[Run-DMC]], and he also worked with [[Slayer]] on early heavy metal crossovers. His stripped-down production style eschews excessive reverb and layering. He produced the American Recordings series that revived [[Johnny Cash]]'s career. In 2007 MTV called him "the most important producer of the last 20 years."
